{{Short description|Musical mass by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart}} {{DISPLAYTITLE:''Great Mass in C minor'', K. 427}} {{Use dmy dates|date=August 2020}} {{Infobox musical composition | name = ''Great Mass in C minor'' | type = Unfinished [[List of masses by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart|missa solemnis
by W. A. Mozart]] | image = 2236 - Salzburg - Erzabtei St Peter.JPG | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Interior of [[St Peter's Abbey, Salzburg]], where the mass was first performed | other_name = | occasion = | catalogue = [[Köchel catalogue|K.]] 427/417a | performed = {{Timeline-event|date={{Start date|1783|10|26|df=y}}|location=[[Salzburg]]}} | published = | vocal = {{plainlist| * [[SATB|{{abbr|SATB|soprano, alto, tenor and bass}}]] double chorus * soloists: 2 sopranos, tenor, bass }} | instrumental = orchestra }} '''''Great Mass in C minor''''' ({{langx|de|Große Messe in c-Moll|links=no}}), [[Köchel catalogue|K.]] 427/417a, is the common name of the musical setting of the [[Mass (music)|mass]] by [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]], which is considered one of his greatest works. He composed it in Vienna in 1782 and 1783, aged 24-25, after his marriage, when he moved to Vienna from [[Salzburg]]. The large-scale work, a [[missa solemnis]], is scored for two [[soprano]] soloists, a [[tenor]] and a [[Bass (voice type)|bass]], double chorus and large orchestra. It remained unfinished, missing large portions of the Credo and the complete Agnus Dei. ==Composition and first performance== {{See also|List of masses by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart}} The work was composed during 1782–83. In a letter to his father [[Leopold Mozart|Leopold]] dated 4 January 1783, Mozart mentioned a vow he had made to write a mass when he would bring his then fiancée [[Constanze Mozart|Constanze]] as his wife to Salzburg. Constanze then sang the "Et incarnatus est" at its premiere.{{Cite book|url=http://www.zeno.org/nid/20007749740|first=Alfred|last=Einstein|author-link=Alfred Einstein|title=Mozart. Sein Charakter, sein Werk|chapter=Kirchenmusik|language=de|location=Zurich, Stuttgart|year=1953|pages=362–403}} The first performance took place in [[Salzburg]] on Sunday 26 October 1783 (the twentieth Sunday after Pentecost). Mozart had moved to Vienna in 1781, but was paying a visit to his home town in the company of Constanze, who had not yet met his father or his sister ([[Maria Anna Mozart|Nannerl]]). The performance consisted of just the Kyrie, Gloria, Sanctus and Benedictus, as surviving parts and a score copy from ca. 1800 show. It took place in the Church of [[St Peter's Archabbey, Salzburg|St. Peter's Abbey]] in the context of a [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] [[Mass (liturgy)|mass]]. Mozart's sister's diary mentions that the performers were the entire {{Lang|de|Hofmusik}}, that is the musicians employed at the court of Salzburg's ruler, [[Archbishopric of Salzburg|Prince-Archbishop]] [[Count Hieronymus von Colloredo]] and thus Mozart's former colleagues.{{harvnb|Deutsch|1965|p=219}} There was a rehearsal in the nearby Kapellhaus on 23 October 1783. ==Fragmentary status== {{Multiple image|center|header=Autograph of two of the pages of the mass ("Kyrie")|image1=Great Mass in C minor (Mozart) p1.jpg|width1=250|image2=Great Mass in C minor (Mozart) p2.jpg|width2=250|footer=Larger version of [[Media:Great Mass in C minor (Mozart) p1.jpg|page 1]] (recto) and [[Media:Great Mass in C minor (Mozart) p2.jpg|page 2]] (verso)}} The work is incomplete, missing the Credo movements following the aria Et incarnatus est (the orchestration of the only two surviving ''Credo'' movements being incomplete) and all of the Agnus Dei. The Sanctus and the Benedictus are partially lost and require editorial reconstructions. There is a good deal of speculation concerning why the work was left unfinished. For purposes of modern performances, the editions and completions available are as follows: * {{ill|Georg Alois Schmitt|de}} (1901, [[Breitkopf & Härtel]]) * [[H. C. Robbins Landon]] (1956, [[Ernst Eulenburg (musical editions)|Eulenburg]]), * [[Helmut Eder]] (1985, [[Bärenreiter]]) * [[Franz Beyer (musicologist)|Franz Beyer]] (1989, Amadeus/[[Edition Peters]]) * [[Richard Maunder]] (1990, [[Oxford University Press]]/[[Carus-Verlag]]), * [[Philip Wilby]] (2004, [[Novello & Co|Novello]]) * [[Robert D. Levin|Robert Levin]] (2005, Carus-Verlag) * Frieder Bernius & Uwe Wolf (2016, Carus-Verlag) * Clemens Kemme (2018, Breitkopf & Härtel) * [[Ulrich Leisinger]] (2019, Bärenreiter). The editions by Landon, Eder, Beyer, Maunder and Kemme aim to simply fill out the missing orchestrations and choral parts in the Credo and Sanctus, whereas the editions by Schmitt, Wilby and Levin aim to complete the work by either using movements from other masses or composing new music for the Credo and Agnus Dei through the use of parody or elaboration of period sketches by Mozart. [[Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs]] ([[Musikproduktion Höflich]]) just offers a complete Credo and an Agnus Dei. For the Credo this means a completions of the 'Credo in unum Deum' and the 'Et incarnatus est' and additional music for the rest of the Credo. This edition, therefore, is intended to be used in combination with any other version of the Mass. [[Robert Xavier Rodriguez]] has also completed the Agnus Dei.[http://www.schirmer.com/Default.aspx?TabId=2420&State_2874=2&workId_2874=35027# "Robert Xavier Rodríguez: Agnus Dei (completion of Mozart's Mass in C minor)], [[G. Schirmer Inc.]] Mozart later reused the music from the ''Kyrie'' and ''Gloria'', almost without changes except for the text, in the [[cantata]] ''[[Davide penitente]]'', K. 469. The mass shows the influence of [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Bach]] and [[George Frideric Handel|Handel]], whose music Mozart was studying at this time (see [[Gottfried van Swieten]]).{{cite book |title=Mass in C minor (Urtext) |last=Mozart |first=W. A. |others=Holl, Monika (preface), Thalmann, Gabriele (transl.) |year=2006 |publisher=[[Bärenreiter|Bärenreiter-Verlag]] |location=[[Kassel]] |pages=VII–X }} ISMN M-0006-20223-2 On 20 August 2016 the version reconstructed by [[Helmut Eder]] was performed at the [[Royal Albert Hall]], for the first time as part of [[The Proms]] series, by the [[BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra]] and [[BBC Symphony Chorus]], with [[Ilan Volkov]] conducting and featuring [[Louise Alder]], [[Carolyn Sampson]], Benjamin Hulett and [[Matthew Rose (bass)|Matthew Rose]].{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b07pdxhs|title=Prom 46: Mahler's Ruckert-Lieder and Mozart's Mass in C minor, 2016, BBC Proms |publisher=bbc.co.uk |date=20 August 2016 |access-date=20 August 2016}} ==Discography == * [[Ferenc Fricsay]], [[Berlin Radio Symphony Orchestra (East Berlin)|Berlin Radio Symphony Orchestra]], Chor der [[St. Hedwig's Cathedral|St.-Hedwigs-Kathedrale]] Berlin, [[Maria Stader]], [[Hertha Töpper]], [[Ernst Haefliger]], Ivan Sardi.
